articles.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
articles.summary: Why is Poundland closing down, and what will happen to staff and suppliers?
articles.body:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

4. Will shoppers still be able to buy from Poundland?

From 26 November you will not get a refund for goods if you change your mind about the purchase. If the item is faulty you will still get a refund.

The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers.

This meant that stock was running low at Poundland.

But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term.

If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it.

5. How will Poundland's collapse change the High Street?

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait; Tehran denies involvement
articles.summary: Two Italian nationals were killed on Thursday in an Iranian drone attack on the Gulf nation of Kuwait, Italy’s Foreign Minister said. Tehran denied any involvement in the incident.
articles.body: Two Italian nationals were killed on Thursday in an Iranian drone attack on the Gulf nation of Kuwait, Italy’s Foreign Minister said. Tehran denied any involvement in the incident. Antonio Tajani said “several drones of Iranian origin targeted Kuwaiti military installations” including an “air defence detection station where two Italian technicians from (Rome-based defense company) Rheinmetall Italia were working.” “A powerful explosion occurred, and, according to reports reaching us from Kuwait, both of our fellow citizens have unfortunately died,” Tajani said in a statement. Kuwait’s defense ministry said its armed forces detected and engaged several hostile drones in Kuwaiti airspace. The ministry blamed what it called “Iranian aggression” for an attack on a “vital site,” saying falling shrapnel wounded two other people, a Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national. Material damage also occurred as a result of the drone attack, it said. The defense ministry confirmed the two deaths and extended its “deepest condolences to the families of the deceased.” Iran denied carrying out the attack. Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Shekarchi, a senior spokesperson for Iran’s armed forces, said: “No military or offensive operations whatsoever have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region.” He claimed it was a “false flag” operation aimed at escalating regional insecurity. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied any Iranian involvement during a phone call with his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. Araghch also “announced Tehran’s readiness to cooperate with the governments of Kuwait and Italy to clarify the origin of the incident and examine its various aspects.” Speaking to reporters later Thursday, Tajani said the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran. Referring to Araghchi’s denial of Iranian responsibility, Tajani noted that “numerous pro-Iranian militias operate in the region.” The Italian technicians were in Kuwait to maintain “detection antennas” for an air defense system used by the country’s armed forces, Italy’s foreign ministry said. In response to the latest attack, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her “deepest sympathy” and offered her “heartfelt condolences” to the victims’ families, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the incident shows how Iran’s “unchecked aggression threatens stability and security in the Middle East and beyond.” Iran has continues to target what it says are American targets in the region in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian sites. Earlier this month, Iran targeted a Kuwaiti air base that hosts US forces after the US military hit what it said was a missile launch site in Iran. Elsewhere, Bahrain on Sunday said an Iranian attack injured at least two people. This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Tommy Robinson charged with failing to give phone Pin to police at Heathrow airport
articles.summary: Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 14 December.
articles.body:
Far-right activist Tommy Robinson has been charged with failing to provide his phone's pin code to police at Heathrow Airport.

The alleged incident happened when Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was detained after returning to the UK from Russia via Turkey on 13 June this year.

The 43-year-old is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 14 December, the Metropolitan Police said.

Posting on X after being charged, Robinson, describing himself as a journalist, said he "refused the Pin because it held private messages from grooming gang survivors".

He described the charge as "pure state persecution".

Robinson, from Bedfordshire, was detained under the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019 in June and has been charged under the same act.

Prior to his arrival in the UK Robinson posted a video on X showing him meeting Elon Musk's father in Moscow.

Robinson is currently awaiting sentencing after being convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found him guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.

Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 December.

Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

articles.title: Israel intensifies assassinations in Gaza as US urges Netanyahu to proceed with ceasefire plan
articles.summary: Israel has intensified its campaign of targeted assassinations in Gaza, striking and killing Hamas commanders and political leaders, as the Trump administration urges Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to proceed with the US-brokered ceasefire plan.
articles.body: Israel has intensified its campaign of targeted assassinations in Gaza, striking and killing Hamas commanders and political leaders, as the Trump administration urges Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to proceed with the US-brokered ceasefire plan. On Thursday, the Israeli military killed Khaled Abu Nada, a senior member of Hamas’ Political Bureau and the organization’s Deputy Minister of Education, in a strike in central Gaza. According to a statement from Hamas, the strike on his residential apartment also killed his wife. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the killing of Abu Nada would disrupt Hamas’ “financial operations and its ability to formulate economic policy.” Hamas said the attack was the result of Israel’s “policy of systematic assassinations” and warned that “targeting civilian homes constitutes a continuous breach of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza and a flagrant violation of all international and humanitarian laws, norms, and conventions.” Since the nominal ceasefire was signed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza to target Hamas. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israeli strikes or military operations over that period. In recent weeks, Israel has escalated those strikes. On Wednesday, Israel struck and killed Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, the head of Hamas’ internal security apparatus in northern Gaza. A day earlier, the IDF killed al-Aouf’s commander, Naeem Muhammad Abu Nahal, who led Hamas’ internal security across Gaza. In each of these cases, the IDF said the assassination was a “blow” to Hamas’ leadership capabilities, even as the militant organization has firmly entrenched its power in the half of Gaza not occupied by the Israeli military. The previous week, the IDF carried out strikes nearly every day targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, from platoon leaders to commanders of Nukhba, a special force within Hamas’ military wing. In each case, the IDF issued virtually the same justification: “Throughout the war, and particularly recently, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, in systematic violation of the ceasefire.” Hamas blamed both Israel and the US-backed Board of Peace for the ongoing attacks. The group said the board “bears political and moral responsibility for the continuation of these crimes as a result of its silence and failure to halt the aggression, and its continued provision of cover and support to the occupation.” The board was established by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution to advance the Gaza ceasefire plan signed in October 2025. But the plan stalled within weeks of its implementation, and much of Gaza remains in ruins. Globally isolated On Tuesday, Netanyahu spoke by phone with Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, who played a crucial role in crafting the ceasefire deal, according to an Israeli source who said they discussed Gaza. According to Axios, Kushner urged Netanyahu to carry out Israel’s obligations under the ceasefire plan, which would require Israel to stop striking Gaza and begin withdrawing forces that occupy more than half of the enclave’s territory. But Netanyahu has refused to make progress on the 20-point plan until Hamas is completely disarmed. Last week, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that Israel “will not withdraw from the current lines of the security zones” until Hamas is “dismantled.” He also warned that Israel is ready to occupy more of Gaza. Hamas has refused to unilaterally disarm, saying that it would only do so alongside a staged Israeli withdrawal from Gaza In an extensive interview with New York magazine, Kushner warned that Israel was increasingly becoming globally isolated. “I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, (and) be much more secure and much more integrated in the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global pariah status,” he said. In another interview, with Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, Kushner called Netanyahu someone who “doesn’t always make it easy” to make progress in the Trump administration’s Gaza plan, and delivered his sharpest rebuke of Israel’s broader posture, arguing it should drop its “constant wartime mindset” and embrace economic diplomacy like Gulf Arab states do. But Netanyahu has not shown any willingness to make concessions toward Gaza to advance the ceasefire agreement, particularly as his far-right allies have advocated for more strikes in Gaza and Palestinian emigration from the shattered territory. On Wednesday, Kushner said in a podcast interview that Israel “needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset and focus on economic diplomacy.” CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this article.

articles.title: Travelers roast the worst passenger offenses they've endured at 30,000 feet
articles.summary: From loud phone calls to smelly snacks, the worst etiquette mistakes on planes are being widely debated online. A former flight attendant weighs in on the most offensive behavior.
articles.body: As the holiday season begins, travelers are taking to social media to call out the most offensive etiquette mistakes they've seen on planes — and there are some surprising contenders. From aisle sprinters to loud talkers, the so-called rude travelers have one thing in common: they forget they're in a shared space. "Passengers will oftentimes forget to pack their manners, and they'll take their frustrations out on flight attendants, and that is just not fair," Jacqueline Whitmore, founder of Protocol School of Etiquette in Palm Beach, Florida, and a longtime etiquette expert, told Fox News Digital. PASSENGER DEFENDS CONTROVERSIAL 'GATE LICE' BEHAVIOR AS AIRLINES CRACK DOWN ON EARLY BOARDING ATTEMPTS Flyers have been taking to Reddit this November to debate the offensive behavior. "What is an unwritten rule of airplane or airport etiquette that more people need to follow?" one Reddit user asked. "The window seat controls the shade. Not the middle seat, not the aisle, and not 4A 20 rows in front," one commenter responded. "Stay seated until the aisle has cleared to your row. I don't want to smell your butt as you are standing next to me for 5 minutes," another said, referring to exiting the plane once it lands. MAJOR AIRLINE ROASTS PASSENGERS WHO JUMP UP RIGHT AFTER LANDING, IGNITING FIERCE BACKLASH Many commenters complained about passengers who do not use headphones. "Not only is it rude to FaceTime or watch Instagram or whatever without headphones, it is also against [the] policy of every airline," said another commenter. "No one should hear the sounds coming out of your phone. Even if you’re a child." Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel expert and author of the blog "View From The Wing," agreed. "Recognize that this is a shared space," he said. "If you're going to have conversations, keep them at an acceptable level. Listen to headphones when you're watching a show or listening to music. ... Keep all of these things to yourself." MAN TRIGGERS RELATIONSHIP CRISIS BY GRABBING FIRST CLASS, LEAVING WOMAN BEHIND IN COACH Leff joked that taking a shower is important, too. "Come to the aircraft having taken your shower that day. Don't go through your personal grooming on board the aircraft," he said. Whitmore, a former flight attendant, ranked other offenses higher. "Back in the day when I was a flight attendant, we'd serve beef and chicken, and we'd have the carts that went up and down the aisle. Now you're lucky if you get a pack of pretzels and some goldfish," she said. "Any time you bring a smelly food on [board the plane], that's offensive because the cabin is a small, shared space," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Taking up too much overhead bin space and using the wrong overhead bin space also topped Whitmore's list. "Another offense that I see is people taking up bin space that doesn't belong to them. A lot of times, they'll come on board, and they'll put their bag in an overhead bin that is way up in the front," she said. "Passengers will oftentimes forget to pack their manners." "If you're going to bring on your roller board, put it above your seat. If there's no space, then you have to find another space in the back." Aisle sprinters — passengers who stand up, grab their bags and rush toward the front of a plane to exit before rows ahead of them — are often criticized too. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "A lot of people will jump up right after the plane lands," said Whitmore. "Technically, they're not supposed to leave their seat until the plane is finished taxiing and has come to a complete stop." She said aisle sprinters have different agendas. Some want to stretch their legs. Others are worried about making a connecting flight. "Some people have tight connections. Please let them pass by," she said. Bare feet and seat kickers always get honorable mentions. Another major offense: standing too close to the baggage claim conveyor carousel. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Don’t stand immediately next to conveyor belts, in security or baggage claim, to be reunited with your luggage," one Reddit user said. "If everyone stands back until their bag is in sight, it lets people actually claim their items without jostling everyone around them." A second commenter agreed, saying, "I hate the way everyone crowds the luggage carousel." Leff urged travelers to remain calm during crowded holiday travel. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The time flyers are on a plane is "ultimately a very short period of time relative to everything else we're going to be doing over the holidays," he said. "We will get through it."

articles.title: UN ruling disputes Israeli allegations used to dismiss UNRWA Gaza staff
articles.summary: Tribunal raises questions about the credibility of UNRWA’s decision to dismiss its staff without substantiated evidence.
articles.body:
A United Nations tribunal has cast doubt on evidence used by UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, to dismiss staff in 2024, finding that the decision was based almost entirely on unsubstantiated allegations by the Israeli government.

UNRWA dismissed nine Palestinian employees in January 2024 after allegations by Israel that they had participated in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

The UNRWA Dispute Tribunal, an impartial tribunal within the UN, noted that the UN’s internal investigation did not include testimonies from the 19 staff members whom Israel accused of involvement in the attacks, according to the judgement seen by Al Jazeera on Thursday.

The judgement said “safety and security concerns” meant that the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) “was not able to interview the 19 staff members and afford them usual due process to respond to the allegations”.

The tribunal also said the allegations against the workers were “based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession”.

“That information has remained in the custody of Israeli authorities and they alone have remained privy as to exactly how it was collected, by whom, when, and where,” it said.

The tribunal also expressed doubts over telephone conversations and messages that Israel claimed to have intercepted and presented as evidence of the staff members’ involvement in the attacks, including with someone “identified by Israeli officials as a Hamas operative”.

“OIOS did not confirm in the investigation report that it was satisfied that the caller was a Hamas operative or that the ‘user’ of the receiving phone was the Applicant,” the judgement said.

It added that one of the Israeli claims of an alleged intercepted phone call between a Hamas operative and a UNRWA staff member was with a duplicated SIM card, which is common in Gaza. “It was determined that the comments made in intercepted calls related to that SIM card were not made by the UNRWA staff member as initially alleged,” the judgement said.

The tribunal’s ruling, dated November 11, found that UNRWA had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to dismiss one of the nine employees, identified as Abu Awad.

The tribunal described Israeli evidence as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability” and awarded Awad a year’s pay and $5,000 in compensation for “moral damages”.

The ruling raises questions about the credibility of the decision by UNRWA, the main humanitarian organisation operating in Gaza, to dismiss its Palestinian staff on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the attacks committed by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.

In January 2024 after consulting UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, former UNRWA Commissioner General Philippe Lazzarini decided that the agency would terminate the contracts of nine staff members.

Their termination letters informed them that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”.

The dismissal decisions were confirmed after a UN investigation that concluded they were likely to have been involved in the October 7 attacks.

Reports have suggested that Lazzarini and Guterres likely made this decision in the hopes that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work in Gaza to continue.

But UNRWA still experienced critical funding cuts from donors. About 600 of its staff members were laid off, salaries in Gaza were cut by 20 percent and aid access remained blocked by Israel amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in the enclave.

articles.title: China, others bash Trump’s latest tariff gambit: ‘Trade wars serve no one’s interests’
articles.summary: Several countries hit by the Trump administration’s new wave of tariffs — which targeted China, the European Union and others — condemned the announcement, arguing the move wouldn’t benefit anyone. “Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Thursday. China could face 20 percent import tariffs…
articles.body:
Several countries hit by the Trump administration’s new wave of tariffs — which targeted China, the European Union and others — condemned the announcement, arguing the move wouldn’t benefit anyone.

“Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Thursday .

China could face 20 percent import tariffs after the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative accused the country of engaging “in acts, policies, and practices that relate to structural excess capacity and production, overwhelming the industries and markets of other economies.”

“So-called industrial overcapacity does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” he continued. “China and the U.S. need to jointly deliver on the important common understandings between the two presidents and maintain the steady growth momentum of China-U.S. economic and trade ties.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced Wednesday that the administration would be implementing a new round of tariffs on China, the EU, Switzerland, Japan, India and others, arguing those nations had developed manufacturing and economic policies that hurt domestic manufacturing in the U.S. and created an unequal trading field globally.

Greer targeted the nations over issues like “inadequate labor protections”; “long-standing industrial plans and targeting”; “support to state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms”; and “policies to promote production and exports with high volumes of export credit,” among other factors.

Criticism from the affected countries was swift.

“We will study the findings,” Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesperson for the European Commission, said in a statement . “At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity.”

“The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” Gill added.

The Department of Commerce under India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry also refuted the idea it had “structural excess capacity.”

“India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement,” the department wrote on social media Wednesday. “It has been India’s position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations.”

Minoru Kihara, Japan’s chief Cabinet secretary, likewise refuted the U.S.’s allegations and called the move “regrettable,” according to The Associated Press .

The move threatens to roil the U.S.’s already fragile economy. The high price of goods stemming from the war in Iran and Trump’s tariff war with Canada led to sweeping gains for Democrats in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month.

articles.title: Oscar-nominated Iranian screenwriter and activist Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran
articles.summary: Leading Iranian rights activist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian was arrested at his home in Tehran, a friend and Europe-based activist said.
articles.body: Leading Iranian rights activist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian was arrested at his home in Tehran on Wednesday, a friend and Europe-based activist told The Associated Press on Thursday. The reasons for the arrest of Mahmoudian, who was one of the screenwriters of the Iranian drama “It Was Just an Accident,” were not clear and there was no official statement from Iranian authorities. Mahmoudian’s personal social media channel on Telegram said agents had arrived at his home on Wednesday, detained him and seized his electronic devices. His detention was also reported on Wednesday by reformist news outlet Emtedad. Hosein Razzagh, a friend of Mahmoudian and an Iranian activist based in Europe, told the AP he last spoke with Mahmoudian by phone at around 2-3 a.m. Wednesday about a death penalty case linked to the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini. He said the screenwriter later didn’t answer his phone, and that witnesses reported that more than a dozen armed agents had raided his home, detained him and taken away his electronic devices. The 2022 protests were sparked by the death of 22-year-old Amini after she was arrested by Iran’s morality police over allegedly not wearing her headscarf correctly. The monthslong crackdown on the protests left hundreds of people dead and thousands detained. Mahmoudian’s detention on Wednesday came a day after he posted on his Telegram channel a warning that two protesters jailed after the Amini protests were at risk of execution within 24 hours. The Oslo-based Iran Human Rights group has said at least 15 protesters have been executed in connection with the protests over Amini, with two of the executions being carried out in 2026. The U.N. Special Rapporteur Mai Sato posted on X later that day regarding the case of Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran, highlighting fears that they were “scheduled to be executed at dawn tomorrow.” But on Wednesday, Mahmoudian posted again on his Telegram channel that according to a lawyer and family, the sentences had not been carried out. Mahmoudian has campaigned openly on behalf of jailed protesters and protesters at risk of execution in Iran, Razzagh said, adding that Iranian authorities “are extremely sensitive about execution cases.” He is being held at the Greater Tehran Penitentiary, just outside of the capital, Razzagh added. The screenwriter was also arrested in February, shortly before the Academy Awards, days after he and 16 others signed a statement condemning Islamic Republic leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the government’s violent crackdown on demonstrators following mass anti-government protests in January. Authorities continue to make arrests linked to the January protests and have stepped up executions of jailed protesters, with at least 39 executions carried out so far, according to rights monitors outside of Iran.

articles.title: Mandelson kept lobby firm shares for months as US ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
articles.summary: The peer was sacked as ambassador last year over his relationship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
articles.body:
Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026 , the same month the company went into administration.

Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".

Ahead of a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.

The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".

The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep – at least in the public policy-interested world outside government – that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."

Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers.

On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle.

He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment.

He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.

He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."

Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."

He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.

Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.

A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.

articles.title: In 2001, a fuel leak drained an Air Transat Airbus A330 over the Atlantic; with both engines out, its pilots glided about 65 nautical miles to the Azores, and 18 people were injured during the evacuation
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of Air Transat Flight 236, where pilots skillfully glided an Airbus A330 to safety after a catastrophic fuel leak led to engine failures over the Atlantic Ocean, injuring 18 during the emergency evacuation.
articles.body: On August 24, 2001, Air Transat Flight 236 was travelling from Toronto to Lisbon when a fuel leak began draining its tanks over the Atlantic Ocean. 293 passengers and 13 crew members were on board the Airbus A330-243. According to the investigation report, the crew struggled to understand why the aircraft’s fuel readings were changing so drastically for over an hour. Eventually, they diverted towards the Azores, but the situation at hand got worse before they could reach land. At first, one engine stopped, then the other. With both engines stopped, the pilots had to guide the aircraft towards Lajes Airport on Terceira Island. While the aircraft landed safely, 18 people were injured during the emergency evacuation.The fuel leak was caused by a maintenance errorThe aircraft had taken off from Toronto with around 46.9 tonnes of fuel on board. Investigators subsequently established that the leak began at around 4:38 am UTC, that is, approximately three hours and 46 minutes into the flight. Fuel started leaking from a fuel-line rupture in the right engine, and the leak rate increased as the journey progressed.The damage was traced back to maintenance work performed before the flight. The right engine had reportedly been replaced, but the installation involved components from different modifications and configurations. According to the investigators, they found that a fuel tube and a hydraulic pressure line had been fitted in an incompatible arrangement. These lines interfered with each other, and the pressurised hydraulic line came into contact with the fuel tube. Therefore, repeated friction caused damage, which ultimately led to a fatigue fracture through which the fuel started leaking.Following the takeoff, at about 5:03 am, the pilots noticed unusual oil pressure and temperature indications from the right engine. At 5:33 am, a fuel imbalance advisory appeared, thus drawing attention to a difference between the quantities in the two wing tanks. The crew present in the flight initially investigated the imbalance. They considered several explanations but could not pinpoint the actual cause.The crew’s fuel management decisions further complicated the situation. They opened the cross-feed system and changed the fuel-pump configuration in an attempt to manage the imbalance between the two tanks and keep the engines supplied. At separate points, the fuel from the left-wing tanks was allowed to feed the right engine, meaning that fuel from those tanks could also escape through the damaged line. The leak, however, still continued despite the crew changing the configuration. At 5:45 am, they decided to divert to Lajes as they realised that the remaining fuel was insufficient to continue to Lisbon.Both engines failed over the AtlanticAt 6:13 am, while the aircraft was about 150 nautical miles from Lajes, the right engine flamed out. Air traffic control was informed of the same, and the aircraft continued towards the Azores using the remaining engine. At 6:23 am, the first officer declared a Mayday. Three minutes later, at an altitude of 34,500 feet and about 65 nautical miles from Lajes, the left engine stopped working as well.The investigation report noted that the pilots began an engines-out descent towards the island with assistance from Lajes air traffic control. They had to manage the aircraft’s altitude and speed while getting ready for the possibility of ditching in the ocean. Meanwhile, inside the cabin, the loss of engine power had affected the aircraft’s electrical systems. Emergency lighting came on, and oxygen masks were deployed after cabin pressure was lost. The crew prepared passengers for an emergency landing, while controllers on the ground guided the aircraft towards the airport.At approximately 6:45 am, the A330 reached Lajes and landed on runway 33. The aircraft touched down at a higher-than-normal speed. Small fires reportedly developed around the left main landing-gear wheels but were quickly put out by the rescue crew present at the runway.The emergency evacuationThe captain ordered an emergency evacuation after the aircraft came to a halt. Passengers and crew left through the emergency exits and evacuation slides. However, one exit did not operate as intended, thus requiring people in that area to use other exits. The evacuation was completed in 90 seconds, and while no fatalities were reported, 16 passengers and two cabin crew members sustained injuries.The findings of the investigation pointed to the incompatible installation of the fuel and hydraulic lines as the technical origin of the leak. Furthermore, it highlighted other operational factors like the crew’s difficulty in recognising the fuel loss and responding to it effectively. Its findings prompted safety recommendations concerning fuel-leak detection, warning systems, pilot training and maintenance procedures.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Trump, NATO chief urge Russia not to expand war in Ukraine
articles.summary: President Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged Russia not to expand its war with Ukraine, as peace talks between the countries have made little headway in recent weeks and as the conflict nears five years. Trump and Rutte, following a meeting Wednesday at the president’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, released a joint statement calling…
articles.body:
President Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged Russia not to expand its war with Ukraine , as peace talks between the countries have made little headway in recent weeks and as the conflict nears five years.

Trump and Rutte, following a meeting Wednesday at the president’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, released a joint statement calling their discussion “outstanding” and “very impactful.” The duo said the Russia-Ukraine war and operation in Iran were “the primary subjects,” while they also talked about “all of the record setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in The Hague and at Ankara.”

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the pair added.

The leaders also spoke about increasing defense spending.

The president, in a Thursday morning post on Truth Social , said he updated Rutte on his discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin during last week’s summit in China , where he pressed Putin to “pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe.”

“I really believe this is a strong possibility — Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” he wrote of the prospects for a peace deal.

Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping issued a four-point “declaration toward peace” last week, pledging to engage in dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation. The declaration, however, made no mention of the war in Ukraine.

The U.S. mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month between Russia and Ukraine, which resulted in an agreed prisoner swap between the two sides but failed to move the needle toward ending the war itself.

“Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, others we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a good first step,” Jared Kushner, U.S. special envoy for peace and Trump’s son-in-law, said.

Kushner praised Putin in a recent interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner, saying the Russian leader “has showed restraint,” adding he has “agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing.”

At the same time, both countries have engaged in tit-for-tat strikes.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, has signaled he could turn to congressional Democrats for additional support when they assume control of both chambers in January, should Trump’s diplomatic efforts falter. He has also called for tougher sanctions against Moscow to bring Russia to the negotiating table.

Trump recently urged Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries , while Putin reportedly vowed to retaliate against Ukraine over the strikes on its energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Putin’s complaints earlier this week, arguing the Russian leader could put an end to the strikes by ending the war.

“Stop complaining. End the war,” Sybiha wrote Tuesday on social platform X.

articles.title: Pregnant inmate escapes from New Mexico corrections facility
articles.summary: Authorities are searching for a pregnant inmate who escaped from a New Mexico corrections facility on Wednesday.
articles.body: A multi-agency search is underway for a pregnant inmate who escaped while being transported from a New Mexico corrections facility Wednesday, while officers stopped to eat. Rebecca Taylor, a woman incarcerated on multiple theft and burglary charges, escaped while being transported from a prenatal appointment in Albuquerque back to the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants, N.M. about 80 miles away. During the transport, Taylor was able to take control of the Dodge Journey SUV she was being taken in and drove away, the New Mexico Corrections Department said in a statement on Facebook. The vehicle was later located by GPS in the Alamosa neighborhood of Albuquerque. Taylor was not inside the vehicle when it was located, the department said. The Santa Fe New Mexican reported that Taylor, 26, escaped while her transporting officers were stopped at a Whataburger restaurant about 11:35 a.m. local time. Taylor was able to unbuckle herself, get in the driver’s seat and drive off, the outlet said, citing a public information officer. That representative declined to comment on the report. A second inmate was in the vehicle but was able to exit and is now in custody, the outlet reported. Late Wednesday, the orange jumpsuit Taylor was wearing was located at an intersection on the city’s west side, the department said. Multiple search teams were actively following up on leads and checking Greyhound buses, Amtrak trains, and other public transportation options, it said. Taylor has ties to Texas in addition to the Albuquerque area. Individuals have been advised that if they spot Taylor to not approach her and instead call 911. “Wanted individuals can be unpredictable and may react in unexpected ways when approached or confronted,” the department said.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s corruption trial: Is it really all over?
articles.summary: Court recommendations put the Israeli leader’s trial, political future and efforts to evade prosecution back in focus.
articles.body:
Benjamin Netanyahu got a boost on Wednesday , when judges in his long-running corruption trial recommended dropping the most serious case against him.

Netanyahu, who has been Israel’s caretaker prime minister since October’s election , is fighting to maintain political power as his rival Gadi Eisenkot tries to build a coalition.

He has also been fighting three corruption cases since 2020, when proceedings against him for bribery, fraud and breach of trust began.

In his telling, the trial has dogged his political career, prevented him from forming a government during a chaotic period of repeated elections between 2019 and 2022 and was responsible for “years of terrible suffering” for himself and his family during the investigation and trial.

Much of the evidence against Netanyahu rests on his efforts to secure favourable coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, in the national media.

The first, Case 1000, relates to accusations that he and his wife received gifts and payments in return for political favours. The second, Case 2000, concerns accusations that he struck a deal with Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth, whereby he would legislate to limit the commercial activities of their rival Israel Hayom in return for favourable coverage. Another, Case 4000, relates to accusations that he granted favours to telecommunications company Bezeq in return for positive coverage for himself and his wife on a news site owned by the telecoms company’s chair.

Judges, who do not have the power to drop charges themselves, have recommended that the Attorney General and Netanyahu critic Gali Baharav-Miara drop Case 4000, saying the prospects of securing a conviction were low, particularly over the bribery allegations. They also expressed doubts about whether the conduct alleged in Case 2000 constituted a criminal offence – and called for the matter to be reconsidered.

In relation to Case 1000, the judges suggested that prosecutors and the defence seek an agreement to bring the proceedings to a conclusion, although a verdict remained another option.

“The judges’ intervention is unprecedented in its nature,” said Barak Medina, legal scholar at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. “They expressed their views before the prosecution had an opportunity to present its arguments.”

So, is this the end of the matter? Will Netanyahu continue to carry the taint of alleged criminality, and how might his career be affected?

Is Attorney General Baharav-Miara likely to drop the case?

It looks likely, but it is still too early to tell.

Responding to the judges’ suggestions, she said, “Every statement and proposal raised just now by the court” will be considered.

“We are open to examining everything. Including things that were argued in the past,” she said.

At the end of her remarks, the attorney general turned to the proposal by Netanyahu’s lawyers that proceedings be concluded through some kind of deal.

“We did this and were ready to accept his proposal, and we responded positively. Our extended hand remains.”

Baharav-Miara and Netanyahu are longstanding political opponents.

Baharav-Miara was among the staunchest critics of Netanyahu’s attempts to overhaul the judiciary and unshackle his government from judicial oversight in the early months of 2023.

She has subsequently challenged several government policies and decisions, including measures affecting the independence of the civil service, and attempts to dismiss the head of Israel’s internal Shin Bet security agency, Ronen Bar .

The Netanyahu-led coalition repeatedly accused her of obstructing its agenda and voted unanimously to dismiss her in August 2025, a decision later overturned by the Supreme Court.

In a defiant speech calling for the trial to end following the judges’ recommendations, Netanyahu said: “The boycotts must end, and now.”

He was referring to the refusal of opposition politicians to work with him due to his case.

“I know what enormous and immediate dangers the state of Israel faces,” he continued. “There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them. We must unite to secure the future of Israel – no less than that, and immediately.”

None of Israel’s main opposition politicians have yet commented on the judges’ advice.

Roi Zur, an Israeli academic at the University of Essex, said the main problem with allying with Netanyahu was not the corruption trial, but rather “ Netanyahu’s role in October 7 and the war that happened afterwards”.

“I don’t think a coalition with Netanyahu becomes more probable. [Naftali] Bennett, who was more open to such a coalition in the last two weeks, is still open to it, whilst the other three party leaders – Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan – still seem to be against such a coalition,” he said.

Netanyahu has been accused of enacting government policies to derail his criminal proceedings. These include claims that he has prolonged the genocidal war on Gaza, putting his political survival ahead of Palestinian lives, a ceasefire and a deal to return Israeli captives.

The accusations intensified during his 2023 judicial overhaul, which opposition politicians, legal figures and protest movements argued would weaken judicial independence and provide Netanyahu with an escape route from prosecution.

In February 2023, former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit accused Netanyahu of pursuing the overhaul to bring his corruption trial to an improper end. Justice Minister Yariv Levin, the reforms’ architect, acknowledged that Netanyahu’s indictments had helped persuade the public of the need for judicial change.

The accusations extended to the conduct of the war on Gaza.

In May 2024, Defence Minister Yoav Gallant urged Netanyahu to put national priorities ahead of personal interests, criticising his lack of a post-war plan. A month later, Benny Gantz, then his principal political rival, accused him of obstructing a captive-release deal for political reasons.

In June 2024, former United States President Joe Biden said there was reason to believe Netanyahu was prolonging the war for political gain, a comment widely interpreted as referring to his corruption trial.

Have other leading Israeli ministers faced similar charges?

Most Israeli prime ministers to have served from 1996 to the present have at some point faced a corruption investigation.

In May 2014, former prime minister Ehud Olmert was convicted of bribery and breach of trust in several corruption cases relating to his time in office and as Jerusalem mayor. He served 16 months in prison.

His successor and Benjamin Netanyahu’s immediate predecessor Ehud Barak, a longstanding ally of disgraced American financier Jeffrey Epstein, was also investigated over allegations of bribery and illegal campaign financing in 2014 but was never charged.

In the late 1990s, Ariel Sharon was investigated over alleged payments to his son in return for political favours in a case known as “the Greek Island Affair” , but prosecutors dropped the case for lack of evidence.

In 2000, Ezer Weizman, who served as Israel’s president and previously as defence minister, was also investigated for corruption. While police said there was enough evidence to support a case of breach of trust and fraud, the statute of limitations had run out. Weizman resigned in July 2000.

articles.body: SRINAGAR: Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk Thursday said Leh district administration summoned him to execute a bond for maintaining peace ahead of Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (LAHDC) elections, scheduled for Dec 4.Though he appeared before the additional district magistrate Thursday, Wangchuk said he refused to sign the peace bond.“This morning after receiving the 19-page show cause notice from the office of additional magistrate in Leh, with a direction to appear before him at 3 pm, I complied and explained informally that there was no question of signing a peace bond or even an interim one since nothing I had said or done could breach peace in any way,” Wangchuk wrote on X.LAB is seeking a deferment of the elections due to harsh weather.“I have sought a week’s time for a formal response since the 19-page notice had many frivolous and unsubstantiated allegations which needed consultation with lawyers and transcription of speeches etc. The hearing was very courteous, and the young Magistrate agreed to one week’s time for reply,” he added.Wangchuk said, however, two hours after they came out, his lawyer received a letter demanding that he submit the reply by Saturday Nov 28. “This is a completely arbitrary and non-transparent process where a notice is served abruptly, and reply is demanded within two days after having clearly agreed to one week.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Romanian lawyer used AI to prepare arguments for Europe’s top human rights court, but fabricated judgments and misleading citations led to a two-year ban on representing applicants
articles.summary: A Romanian lawyer has been barred from representing applicants before the European Court of Human Rights for two years after submitting legal arguments
articles.body: A Romanian lawyer has been barred from representing applicants before the European Court of Human Rights for two years after submitting legal arguments containing fabricated judgments and incorrect citations. The errors came to light when judges examined the documents and found references to rulings that did not exist, along with paragraph numbers that could not be traced to the original decisions. The lawyer acknowledged using artificial intelligence while preparing the submissions but had failed to check the references properly. The court said the inaccuracies went beyond simple mistakes, pointing to a failure to meet the professional standards expected of legal representatives.How AI-generated legal references became a problem in a human rights caseThe matter came to light during the examination of an application before a Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). The Romanian lawyer was one of two representatives acting for the applicants in the proceedings. While reviewing the written observations submitted on behalf of the applicants, the Chamber identified several problems with the legal authorities cited in support of the arguments. Some judgments referred to in the documents did not exist at all. Other references pointed to genuine decisions but included paragraph numbers that could not be found in the original texts.There were also instances in which the lawyer had cited actual European Court of Human Rights judgments that had little relevance to the arguments being made. In some cases, the authorities cited appeared to contradict the very points they were supposed to establish. The mistakes were not confined to a handful of references. The Chamber found a recurring pattern across the submissions, raising concerns about how the legal material had been prepared and checked before it was sent to the court.The lawyer subsequently acknowledged using artificial intelligence tools while drafting the observations. She characterised the problems as inaccuracies and citation errors, but the Chamber considered that description insufficient to explain the scale and nature of what had happened.How unverified AI-generated references became a matter of professional responsibilityA central issue in the proceedings was whether the errors could be treated as isolated oversights or whether they reflected a broader failure to meet the standards expected of a legal representative. The Chamber took the second view. Its examination indicated that the documents contained numerous substantive inaccuracies, including invented judicial decisions and incorrect descriptions of existing case-law. The repeated nature of these problems was an important consideration.The lawyer had admitted that she did not adequately verify every legal reference produced during the drafting process. However, the Chamber considered that even this acknowledgement did not fully reflect the extent of the failure. For several references, it concluded that no meaningful verification had taken place. The judges also pointed out that many of the incorrect citations followed repetitive patterns and could have been identified through a basic search of HUDOC, the European Court of Human Rights' official database of judgments and decisions.What professional standards require of lawyers using AI toolsThe decision also placed the incident within the existing professional obligations governing lawyers in Romania and those representing applicants before the European Court of Human Rights. As per the European Court of Human Rights, the Chamber referred to Romania's Legal Profession Act, Law no. 51/1995, the regulations governing legal practice and the Strasbourg court's own case-law. These establish expectations that lawyers should perform their work with reasonable professional competence.Representation before the ECHR also requires a particularly high degree of care when dealing with legal authorities and arguments submitted for judicial consideration. The Chamber's position was that using AI to prepare legal documents did not remove the representative's responsibility for their contents. Any case-law references or legal propositions generated through such tools needed to be checked independently against reliable material before being presented to the judges.How the inaccurate submissions affected the court proceedingsThe Chamber also examined the practical consequences of the lawyer's conduct. Its concerns extended beyond the quality of the documents and the accuracy of the legal arguments.The incorrect references required the Court to spend considerable time verifying the observations. The Chamber also had to initiate separate proceedings under Rule 44D and correspond extensively with other stakeholders, creating additional work that it considered incompatible with its functions under the Convention.Romanian lawyer excluded for two years under Rule 44DThe exclusion was imposed through Rule 44D of the European Court of Human Rights' Rules of Court, which allows action to be taken against advocates or other representatives in exceptional circumstances. On 13 November 2026, the President of the European Court of Human Rights approved a reasoned proposal submitted by the Chamber handling the application. The decision prevents the Romanian lawyer from representing or otherwise assisting litigants before the court for a period of two years.The process involved more than the Chamber's initial examination of the written observations. Under Rule 44D, the lawyer was given an opportunity to comment on the proposed exclusion. The Romanian Government and the Romanian National Bar Association were also invited to provide their views.Their submissions were exchanged between the parties, who were subsequently allowed to respond to one another's comments. The Iași Bar Association was invited to participate as well but did not submit comments. After considering the material received, the Chamber concluded that the circumstances met the exceptional threshold required for exclusion under the rule. It then forwarded its recommendation to the President of the Court, who accepted it.What happens after the lawyer's two-year ECHR banThe restriction is not necessarily permanent. Rule 44D § 3 provides for the possibility of restoring a representative's rights, and the court has expressly indicated that the present decision does not prevent the lawyer from seeking their reinstatement.The lawyer has been formally notified of the decision and the reasons behind it. The applicants involved in the proceedings, the Romanian Government, the Romanian National Bar Association and the Iași Bar Association have also been informed.The exclusion concerns only one of the two representatives appointed in the underlying case. The other representative is not covered by the measure. The ruling comes as courts continue to deal with the professional responsibilities that arise when lawyers use automated systems to prepare legal documents. In this instance, the European Court of Human Rights focused on the accuracy of the material submitted, the lawyer's failure to verify it and the additional burden placed on the administration of justice.Disclaimer: This article is based on a press release issued by the Registry of the European Court of Human Rights.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nick Saban is suddenly singing a very different tune about winning national championships
articles.summary: Nick Saban says winning a national championship doesn't prove a conference is best, undercutting the SEC arguments as Big Ten teams claim playoff titles.
articles.body: Nick Saban is inarguably one of the best coaches in college football history. His resume is difficult to match, from turning the LSU Tigers around in the early-2000's, ultimately winning a BCS national championship, to making the Alabama Crimson Tide a force of nature throughout the 2010s. His ability to get the most out of his players, keep up defensively as offenses changed and evolved over time, and find and improve assistant coaches turned the Tide into a juggernaut. It's easy to forget now, but until Saban's tenure, Alabama went from 1980-2007 without being ranked number one in the major polls. After winning his first title in Tuscaloosa in 2010, Saban famously said that it wasn't the end, but the beginning of a new run for the Tide. He was right. They won five more championships, including the COVID-adjusted 2020 College Football Playoff. HERE'S HOW BAD THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF'S SELECTION COMMITTEE RANKINGS ACTUALLY ARE Nobody questions Saban's accomplishments, or that Alabama was a dynasty in the Saban era. But one of the most harmful consequences of that time, for the rest of the sport, was that his success created the perception that the SEC was head and shoulders above the other conferences. Winning a title is the ultimate accomplishment, and a reflection on the rest of the conference, the thinking went. And that thinking permeated throughout college football and was used to justify giving the SEC the preferential treatment in the College Football Playoff poll that they enjoy today. Now though? Saban has thoroughly undercut that argument, and the justification for the SEC's obvious benefits, by saying winning a title doesn't determine the best conference. Speaking on "The Pat McAfee Show," Saban said that all those years of the SEC fans saying Alabama's national championship wins made them the best conference in the country was wrong. "Just because you win a national championship does not make and evaluate the level of your league," Saban said. "It means you had a really good team that was better than everybody else, but it doesn’t mean you necessarily had the best league from top to bottom. My argument with the SEC has always been the strength of the league, from top to bottom. I think that’s very clear this year." Interesting! We'll come back to whether he's right or not, at least regarding this season, but what this seems to be is a convenient reshaping of the narrative. If the SEC had won the last three titles, while having little "depth," the Greg Sankey-SEC Network promotional apparatus would be saying that winning a championship is what matters most. But when the Big Ten wins three in a row, without the SEC even reaching the national championship game, it's a different story. Wonder why. NICK SABAN SPEAKS TRUTH ON CFP EXPANSION: ‘THERE’S NOT 24 TEAMS’ THAT CAN WIN A NATIONAL TITLE, BUT MONEY WINS Saban earlier this summer also accidentally undercut this very argument. "I think the only reason people are talking about this is we dominated for so long, and we were so good, everybody makes a big deal out of being able to beat us," he said on SEC Network. "That doesn’t mean they’re better than us, and that doesn’t mean that just because you win the championship that you have a better conference. It just means you have one better team." Ah, so they "dominated," he says. How did they dominate? By winning championships. How do we know? Because the SEC's depth during the Saban era was frequently worse than other conferences. Let's look at the final AP poll after the 2015 season, one of Saban's championship winning seasons, as an example. The Tide finished No. 1, of course, but the next highest SEC team was...Ole Miss at No. 10. There were just two SEC teams in the top-15 of the final poll. Meanwhile, the Big Ten had four teams in the top-15, the ACC had three, and the Big 12 also had three. There were just three SEC teams in the top-20, the same number as the Pac-12. So was the SEC the best and "deepest" conference that season? Or was it just that Alabama won the national championship, which automatically made them the best? CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE It's a similar story in 2017, when only three SEC teams finished in the top-17. The Big Ten had five. The Big 12 also had three. So which is it? Was the SEC the best because Alabama won? Because it certainly wasn't a deeper league. In 2016, only one SEC team finished higher than No. 13 the final poll: Alabama. The Pac-12 had three teams in the top-13, the Big Ten had four. The Big 12 had two. Most seasons, this is how it played out: Alabama was dominant, the rest of the SEC wasn't. Yet the chanting continued anyway, because they were winning championships. Now that they haven't, it's "we're the deeper league." Sure, Nick. And even with championships, going back as far as 2013, the SEC's won six championships, the Big Ten has won four, and the ACC's won three. This season too, Saban's wrong. And we can use more objective measurements than the AP Top 25 poll to show it. ESPN's SP+, an opponent-adjusted ranking system based on offensive, defensive, and special teams efficiency and success rate, has seven Big 12 teams in its latest top-25 ranking. There are six Big Ten teams, five SEC teams, and three from the ACC. So the Big 12 is the deepest conference right now, based on how teams would be expected to perform moving forward, based on opponent-adjusted success rate in the three facets of football. The Big Ten is the second deepest, and the SEC is third. When it comes to top-25 quality teams. If you expand to the top-35, the Big Ten has a whopping 11 teams in that range, while the SEC has eight. And of course, their performance in last year's bowl season shows how much of the "depth" argument is just inaccurate perception. SEC teams were 0-3 against other Power 4 conferences in last year's playoff. They were 1-8 in bowl games. Alabama, the poster child for the SEC's unearned special treatment, were humiliated by Indiana in the Rose Bowl 38-3, after being gifted a spot in the tournament by an atrocious selection committee. As is so often the case in college football, narratives shift based on what's most beneficial at the moment. The SEC this season is better at the top, but weaker in the middle, than the Big Ten or even the Big 12. Yet they still enjoy the benefits of perceived "depth" because of big stadiums and Lane Kiffin complaining. Or Greg Sankey's lecturing and propaganda tours. Or something. They haven't won a championship in the NIL era, while every school is paying players, yet still ride the coattails of Nick Saban's teams from 2009-2017. Though, of course, Georgia may very well win a title this year, in which case, the argument will switch back. If they had teams ranked 1-15 in SP+, and lost the championship, they'd be saying depth is what matters. The one constant? Whatever makes the SEC look best is the ultimate conference measurement.

articles.title: Rocker the Black and Tan Coonhound Wins Best in Show at the 2026 National Dog Show on Thanksgiving Day
articles.summary: The National Dog Show judge called the coonhound “an outstanding example of what the breed standard is right now”
articles.body:
Rocker, a black and tan Coonhound, won his 15th Best in Show title at the National Dog Show

The hound impressed judges with his breed-standard features, athleticism, and hunting abilities

The annual event aired on Nov. 26 and will re-air on NBC November 29

The 2026 National Dog Show has crowned its winner — and Rocker the black and tan Coonhound has taken home the win.

The hound, who came into the competition as the top-ranked for his breed and the fourth-ranked in the Hound Group, nabbed his 15th Best in Show title against the more than 2,000 dogs present at the 25th National Dog Show Presented by Purina. His victory aired on Nov. 26, 2026.

"He is an outstanding example of what the breed standard is right now," Best In Show judge Lorraine Bisso of Metairie, La., said of Rocker's win. "He's just a beautiful dog. He's got a very masculine head. It's correct for the breed in terms of length and width."

He was presented by his handler, Mandy Clevenger, who has worked with the pooch since he began competing in shows at 6 months old. Rocker was also supported by his owner, Traci Mitchell. Bisso further described the dog as an "athlete," noting his ears and feet, in particular, were worthy of praise.

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

"Those long ears actually catch the scent and bring it up to the dog," she explained. "He has beautiful feet. He has a lovely forechest — which is necessary, because he's going to run for 25 miles. Tail is up. I mean, this is a hunting hound."

The show's final round saw Rocker go up against six other dogs who had been crowned the best in their own categories: a Lhasa Apso named "Kissy," a Newfoundland named "Biggie Smalls," a Norfolk Terrier named "Rambo," a Pomeranian named "Aslan," a Curly-Coated Retriever named "Raisin" and a Pembroke Welsh Corgi named "Brandi." Kissy, the Lhasa Apso representing the Non-Sporting Group from Conroe, Texas, was the Reserve Best In Show.

"Over the past 25 years, watching the National Dog Show on Thanksgiving has become a tradition for millions of American families, and it's something every generation can truly enjoy together," said Nina Leigh Krueger, CEO and President at Nestlé Purina North America in a statement to PEOPLE. "It's incredibly humbling to know that something Purina helped create has led to fun moments and fond memories for so many families over the years."

Coverage of the show and Rocker's victorious moments was broadcast on NBC and Peacock Thanksgiving Day. The show will be re-broadcast on NBC Sunday, November 29, from 4 to 6 p.m.
