articles.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
articles.summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
articles.body:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

articles.title: Attack on Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery kills worker, halts some operations
articles.summary: Some operations at Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery were temporarily halted after a hostile aerial projectile struck the facility on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said in a statement.
articles.body: Some operations at Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery were temporarily halted after a hostile aerial projectile struck the facility on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said in a statement. The ministry’s statement did not identify the attacker, but the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said earlier on Thursday that the Iran-aligned group had attacked the refinery. The strike was the Houthis’ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides. The projectile caused a fire that was later brought under control, the ministry said in a statement carried by the Saudi state news agency. Emergency and technical teams had responded to the incident and were assessing damage and checking the safety of facilities, it added. The refinery in the southwestern city of Jazan, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day. The coalition said it had destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in the Yemeni port city of Hodeidah, which it said the Houthis had used in Thursday’s attack on the refinery. Earlier, it warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military response. The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen including the capital Sanaa, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war. The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference. Fighting has intensified since the Houthis seized strategic territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September and advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route for Gulf oil producers seeking access to the Red Sea.

articles.title: Thousands protest in Irbil as Baghdad moves to seize Kurdish oil and border control
articles.summary: IRBIL, Iraq — Thousands of demonstrators gathered Thursday in Irbil, the capital of Iraq’s semiautonomous northern Kurdish region, protesting a move by the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.
articles.body: IRBIL, Iraq — Thousands of demonstrators gathered Thursday in Irbil, the capital of Iraq’s semiautonomous northern Kurdish region, protesting a move by the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced the measures Tuesday, describing them as steps to address oil smuggling. The decision marked a new escalation in a long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities and spurred rival Kurdish parties to come together in opposition to Baghdad. Al-Zaidi — who took office earlier this year with the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump — has been trying to assert authority on several fronts, including sending security forces into an area long controlled by a powerful Iran-backed militia last week. A move to consolidate control Tuesday’s decision brings official and unofficial border crossings in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces to it. Al-Zaidi also dismissed Kirkuk’s operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflect Iraq’s “independent national will.” Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court on Wednesday backed Baghdad’s move and ruled that federal authorities may deploy troops to secure all of Iraq’s international borders, “including the borders located within the territories administered by the Kurdistan Region.” Defense Ministry spokesman Maj. Gen. Yahya Rasool said Wednesday evening that al-Zaidi, who is also commander in chief, had ordered the deployment of military units to Kirkuk and other provinces and had ordered dirt roads used for oil smuggling to be blocked. A long-running power struggle Iraq’s Kurds have governed themselves since 1991, and the 2005 constitution recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But since 2003, Irbil and Baghdad have struggled for control over land, oil and money. The Kurdish regional government’s cabinet said Wednesday that al-Zaidi’s order “violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region” and represents “an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime.” It accused Baghdad of using “military rhetoric and threats” to carry out a “premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.” The Federal Supreme Court said the Kurdish regional government’s authority covers only the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the U.S.-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein. Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week’s orders. The Iraqi constitution’s Article 140 was meant to settle the fate of the disputed territories, a band of land from the Syrian to the Iranian border that is home to Kurds, Arabs, Yazidis, Assyrians, Turkmen and other communities. The article called for reversing Saddam-era policies that expelled Kurds from the area and moved Arabs in. It also called for a census and a referendum by the end of 2007 on whether the areas would join the Kurdistan Region. Neither was held. Peshmerga forces took control of oil-rich Kirkuk in 2014, when the Iraqi army collapsed in the face of an offensive by Islamic State militants. Iraqi forces pushed them out in October 2017, weeks after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum that Baghdad called unconstitutional. Oil at the center of disputes The disputes between Baghdad and Irbil have largely centered around oil exports and revenues. The country relies on oil revenues for about 90% of its budget. In 2014, Baghdad suspended federal budget transfers to the Kurdish region amid a dispute over oil exports. Disagreements over oil revenues and budget allocations have since repeatedly delayed salary payments for public employees in the region. In 2022, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled the Kurdish region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The following year, oil exports through Turkey were suspended after an international arbitration ruling found Turkey had violated its pipeline agreement with Iraq by allowing independent Kurdish oil exports. Exports resumed in 2025 under an agreement placing sales under federal government oversight. The Kurdish region’s own politics are also in turmoil. On Nov. 5, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan quit the government led by the Kurdistan Democratic Party, calling it “failed” and threatening to form a parallel administration. No new cabinet has been formed since October 2024 regional elections, and the legality of the current government is being challenged at the Federal Supreme Court.

articles.title: Democrats’ plan to end funding for Iran war leaves open what comes next
articles.summary: One of the top priorities for the incoming Democratic majorities is cutting off funding for the U.S. war with Iran, which was launched by President Trump nine months ago with no input from Congress. What happens after that — and whether Democrats can force Trump to end the war without jeopardizing U.S. forces in the…
articles.body:
One of the top priorities for the incoming Democratic majorities is cutting off funding for the U.S. war with Iran, which was launched by President Trump nine months ago with no input from Congress.

What happens after that — and whether Democrats can force Trump to end the war without jeopardizing U.S. forces in the region — remains an open question.

“We’re working on a consensus position; we’re not there yet,” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, told The Hill.

One of the first opportunities for Democrats to throttle offensive operations in Iran is coming up even before they retake control of the House and Senate. Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government, which some Democrats see as an opportunity.

A full-year spending bill with Republican support would likely preserve funding for the war at a precarious time, when Trump is alternating between threats to restart offensive military operations and to hold out with sanctions and a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), the ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, has said she’s in favor of full-year spending bills for as many uncontroversial funding priorities as possible.

That could leave open the option for a short-term spending bill on the military, with Democrats addressing the war when they take over the majority in Congress in January.

“To a person, we all want to see the funding on the war ended; the issue is how that gets done, what we can do in the short term and then what we need to do afterward,” DeLauro told reporters last week.

The immediate path forward on Iran is not expected to become clear until after Senate Democrats vote on their caucus leadership Dec. 1.

The contest is between longtime leader Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who has elevated his progressive bona fides over the past few years. This includes his challenging the Biden administration’s policy on Israel.

Van Hollen has called for “not one penny more” in funding for the war. Schumer’s position is unclear.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who is backing Schumer, along with Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who are undecided, announced last week they will move to add an amendment to appropriations bills to block funding for the Iran war.

“This amendment is the bare minimum Congress can do to heed Americans’ call and use our power of the purse to force the President to end this conflict we never should’ve been in,” Duckworth said in a statement.

Some House Democrats also see ending funds for the war immediately as increasing pressure on Trump to pursue diplomacy with Tehran.

“If we end the war, it will force Trump to the negotiating table with Iran,” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a member of the House Armed Services Committee.

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the U.S. needs to advance a diplomatic resolution with Iran.

“The administration needs to come and talk with us and consult with us, and as they continue to work on a diplomatic solution, we all need to be engaged,” she said.

The challenge for Democrats will be preserving funding for the defense of U.S. troops in appropriations bills without letting the administration use those resources for offensive operations on Iran.

“Crafting the language that an administration can’t drive a truck through, and find a loophole, is hard. But I do think it is important,” said Damian Murphy, senior vice president for national security and international policy at the Center for American Progress.

Funding for defense of allies and partners is also a bipartisan priority. But ending funding for major bombing campaigns is important, Murphy argued, blocking the administration from relying on what’s proven to be a failed strategy.

“This idea that you can somehow bomb your way to what you want, this administration has had nine months of time to do that … and it just hasn’t worked,” he said.

“As you look at the ledger, the answer is pretty clear that the first thing that needs to happen is an end to these kinetic operations and a focus on a serious diplomatic pressure track.”

The war is stuck in a fragile and dangerous stalemate. Trump has held off renewing large-scale bombing campaigns amid concerns over munitions shortages for defense for both U.S. assets in the region and Persian Gulf and Arab partners.

Sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade against Iran have helped increase the economic pressure on Iran and allow for some ships to move through the Strait of Hormuz. But danger is ever-present and escalating.

Two oil tankers struck naval mines, causing explosions and fires, in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said in a statement carried by state media. The Guard navy accused the tankers of trying to use a route that avoided Iranian control of the strait.

The mine collisions come as attacks on tankers reached their highest levels in October with 30 ships damaged, CNN reported , and at least 22 attacks on ships in the first three weeks of November.

The persistent attacks on oil tankers are keeping oil prices high, The Wall Street Journal reported , adding that even as other export routes come online, oil price per barrel is expected to be between $85 and $95 — keeping prices high at the pump.

Iran is further projecting defiance, launching limited strikes against U.S. military installations in the Persian Gulf, particularly in Bahrain in recent days. The top commander of the Guard, Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, said in a speech Wednesday that Iran is ready to “drive the enemy” into retreat, according to state-backed media .

Who is leading diplomacy on the U.S. side is up in the air, although it remains fully under Trump’s control.

“Congress can make recommendations and can suggest ideas on that front, can demand oversight on how the diplomacy is going,” Murphy said. “But they can’t actually conduct the diplomacy itself.”

Trump announced earlier this month that he was removing Vice President Vance from talks on the war, after Vance blamed the Republican midterm losses on the conflict.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s close friend and his son-in-law, respectively, have turned their attention away from Iran and toward negotiating an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine. However, the duo reportedly discussed Iran with senior Qatari officials last week in Berlin on the sidelines of meetings about Ukraine.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, has often stayed on the sidelines of the conflict. But he’s increased the pace of calls with Persian Gulf partners in recent days, speaking with his counterparts in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain by phone and holding a meeting with the Qatari prime minister and foreign minister in Washington on Tuesday.

Rubio would be an effective Iran czar but has held back from asserting himself, argued Michael Makovsky, president and CEO of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America.

“He’s the most knowledgeable of any of them. He’s been dealing with the Iran issue for a long time. I think he’s purposely tried not to be out ahead on Iran,” Makovsky said. “My understanding is internally he’s not overly assertive, but he should be.”

articles.title: Two Italians killed in attack on Kuwait site, Iran denies involvement
articles.summary: DUBAI/ROME — Two Italians were killed in a drone attack in Kuwait on Thursday that Italy and Kuwait blamed on Iran, although Tehran has denied any involvement.
articles.body: DUBAI/ROME — Two Italians were killed in a drone attack in Kuwait on Thursday that Italy and Kuwait blamed on Iran, although Tehran has denied any involvement. The two were technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian unit of German defense group Rheinmetall RHMG.DE, and were at an air defense surveillance station in Kuwait when it was targeted by Iranian drones, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Senate in Rome. “Following a powerful explosion, both of our compatriots, according to information coming from Kuwait, have died. Two other people were injured: a Pakistani national and a captain in the Kuwaiti army,” Tajani said. Kuwait‘s Defense Ministry confirmed that the two Italians had died of their injuries, after initially reporting that four people had been wounded by falling debris when a “vital facility” was targeted in what it said was an Iranian attack. It said the other two injured were Kuwaiti and Pakistani nationals and that the attack had caused material damage. Iran’s senior armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi denied that Iran had attacked a “vital” site in Kuwait, saying no offensive or military operations by Iranian forces had taken place in the region, Iranian state media reported on Thursday. Iran’s embassy in Rome also categorically denied the claims of an Iranian drone attack on a military site in Kuwait in a post on X. Tajani told Italian news agency AGI that Italy would lodge a complaint with the Iranian embassy over the incident, urging caution and saying there was no need to attack Arab countries bordering Iran that were not involved in the war. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi denied any Iranian involvement in the attack and said Tehran was prepared to undertake joint investigations with Kuwait “to identify the origin of the incident and parties involved in it”, according to a post on his Telegram channel. The regional conflict erupted on February 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran, and it has since widened to include Iranian strikes on Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military bases. Earlier in November, Iran said it had targeted U.S. drone and missile sites in Kuwait after the United States struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
articles.summary: A New York Times report lends credence to long-held belief that torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.
articles.body:
The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.

Wednesday’s report comes after the newspaper filed a lawsuit to obtain material gathered by special prosecutor John Durham, who was appointed in 2008 to investigate the CIA’s activities.

Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.

The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.

Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.

The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.

While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.

But rights groups have long suspected that such abuses were much more widespread than the CIA admitted. The agency had previously acknowledged waterboarding three detainees.

According to the documents The New York Times received, a contract translator who worked with the CIA observed an additional case of waterboarding.

While the documents do not specify where the translator worked, the newspaper said it determined that the location was likely a black site outside of Bagram Air Force Base on the outskirts of Kabul, Afghanistan.

The translator, The New York Times explained, referenced a detainee death that matched a facility known as Detention Site Cobalt or the “Salt Pit”, which became infamous for abusive conditions.

In an interview with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the translator stated that he had seen a man referred to as “Bashir” facing the torture practice.

He described Bahir as “lying on the board with the head of the board tilted downward into the water”.

“There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the document said, summarising the translator’s statements.

The FBI summary explains that the translator “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself”. The incident allegedly took place in a hallway.

The CIA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of this article’s publication.

The agency has also not acknowledged waterboarding detainees at any site in Afghanistan. The three detainees it has acknowledged torturing were held at black sites in Thailand and Poland.

One was Abu Zubaydah, the first detainee the CIA held in a black-site prison, located in Thailand. The US government for years falsely depicted him as one of the highest-ranking members of al-Qaeda, a group of which he was not a member, according to US intelligence reports.

A 2014 report on the CIA torture programme by the Senate Intelligence Committee found that Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times, sometimes as a means of helping instruct torture methods.

Another was Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of being the architect of the September 11 attacks.

The third was Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, who is accused of helping plan al-Qaeda’s 2000 bombing of a Navy destroyer, the USS Cole.

All three are currently being held in the Guantanamo Bay military prison in Cuba.

articles.title: In Canada, Quebec’s religious symbols ban faces a Supreme Court test
articles.summary: Canada’s top court weighs Bill 21, the Quebec law that shapes where Muslim women can work and where they feel welcome.
articles.body:
Navien Waly had been volunteering at her kids’ schools, helping out at bake sales and serving on graduation committees, for a decade when she received an email informing her that her presence was no longer welcome.

Under Quebec law, it said, parents who wore religious symbols could no longer volunteer.

Waly had started wearing the hijab four years earlier, at age 40.

She said the email felt like a “slap in the face” and that she struggled to respond when her two younger kids, who had got used to their mother’s presence at school, asked what she had done wrong.

“I’m the same person I was 10 years ago,” she said. “It doesn’t make me any different. I’ve never spoken about my religion.”

The law also upended her plans to return to work. Waly, now 45, had left a career in finance to pursue a career as a specialised educator. She was supposed to start work next year, but now, she says she can’t do the work she was trained for as long as she continues to wear the hijab.

The law behind the email, Bill 94, expanded the restrictions that Quebec first introduced under Bill 21 in 2019. On Friday, Canada’s Supreme Court is set to rule on a challenge to that earlier law, which bans public school teachers, police officers and certain other public officials from wearing religious symbols on the job.

The landmark ruling could also clarify how far governments can go in using a provision of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms to shield laws from certain rights challenges.

‘Your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions’

In the seven years since Bill 21 passed, its impacts have been felt across religious minorities but have been particularly devastating for Muslim women.

In a survey conducted in 2022 and 2023 for a report by the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) and York University researcher Nadia Hasan, 73 percent of the 411 Muslim women surveyed said Bill 21 had impacted their job search, while 48 percent believed they didn’t get a job because of their religious identity.

Some women take their hijabs off when they get to work and put them back on when they leave, said National Council of Canadian Muslims chief executive Stephen Brown, adding that he’d spoken to women who described the routine as humiliating.

Being made to choose between “your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions”, Brown said, “was a dehumanising and cruel situation to inflict on people”.

But the consequences of the law extend beyond work. In the same survey, 88 percent of Muslim women said the law had made Quebec a less welcoming place to live.

Brown said some Muslims in Quebec had compared the climate to what they see in France, where it’s “open season on Muslims”.

Waly, who was born and raised in Canada, said in recent years, in the period coinciding with Quebec’s policies on religious symbols and her starting to wear the hijab, “things have happened to me that have never happened before”.

A couple of months ago, she was at a grocery store checkout when a man behind her started singing about how immigrants had ruined his life. He sang that he’d lost his job and been forced to retire at age 30 because of “people like you”. Waly turned around and asked in French if he was talking to her. The man went red, she recalled.

In recent years, she’s encountered more hostile looks and racist comments, with strangers telling her: “Go back to your home.”

Brown said many Muslim Quebecers who speak English and who can take their work elsewhere have left the province or are planning to. For those who only speak French, relocating can be much harder, he said.

People have suggested to Waly that she move to another province, too. But she can’t imagine leaving her family and the place where she grew up. Her father, brothers, nieces and nephews all live in Quebec.

“You can’t, after living here for 45 years, to just uproot your whole life.”

When Quebec introduced Bill 21 in 2019 , the government presented it as a moderate approach to settling the province’s long-running debate over secularism.

The debate goes back to the 1960s Quiet Revolution when Quebec began taking control of public institutions like schools and hospitals away from the Catholic Church.

Decades later, tensions over how those institutions should accommodate religious minorities led to the Bouchard-Taylor commission. The commission recommended that judges, police and others who exercise the coercive power of the state be barred from wearing religious symbols at work.

With Bill 21, the Coalition Avenir Quebec government took things further, bringing public school teachers under the ban. Those who were already in their posts could keep wearing religious symbols as long as they didn’t change jobs or employers.

In an interview with Radio-Canada days after the law passed, Premier Francois Legault defended it, saying the majority had felt ignored on the issue for years. “To avoid extremes, you have to give a bit to the majority,” he said, suggesting the far right would want to take things even further, and stressing that religious symbols could still be worn in the street.

Polling ahead of the law passing found that 64 percent of respondents in Quebec supported the bill.

In Brown’s view, the legislation, which was put together during an election campaign, was about getting votes, tapping into longstanding distrust of organised religion, anti-Muslim sentiment and fears about the future of Quebec’s French-speaking culture.

“You combine those together, and it becomes a really effective wedge when it comes to driving support towards the party during elections,” he said.

In the years since, Quebec has expanded the restrictions beyond the jobs covered by Bill 21.

In 2025, Bill 94 extended the ban on religious symbols to school support staff and volunteers, including parents like Waly. It also required students to keep their faces uncovered at school and barred prayer on school premises.

And earlier this year, Bill 9 extended the symbols ban to include daycare staff, forbade face coverings at Quebec’s public colleges and universities, and restricted where people could pray on campus.

The newly elected Parti Quebecois government has now pledged to ban elementary school students from wearing religious symbols in schools.

What’s at stake in the Supreme Court ruling?

When Quebec passed Bill 21, it used a provision known as the notwithstanding clause, which lets governments keep a law in place even if it violates certain rights protected by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including freedom of religion and the right to equality. That protection lasts up to five years at a time and can be renewed. Quebec renewed it in 2024, saying it was needed to preserve “social peace”.

A Quebec court found in 2021 that the law infringed on the rights of people who wear religious symbols, but upheld most of the law because Quebec had invoked the notwithstanding clause. The Quebec Court of Appeal upheld the ruling in 2024 and reversed an exemption for English-language school boards. The Supreme Court heard the case in March.

The NCCM, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the World Sikh Organization and others are challenging the law. They argue it violates constitutional rights despite Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause.

Brown said the council wants the court to invalidate the use of the clause in this case.

“The notwithstanding clause is supposed to be an extraordinary power of last resort,” he said, arguing it should not be used in cases where “governments are deliberately targeting the rights of citizens for political gain”.

Waly is not optimistic that the court will overturn the law, but is holding out hope that she won’t have to start over.

“At 45 years old, to start thinking of another path? I don’t know what I’m going to do,” she said. “Something’s gotta give.”

But she worries about her kids, who are now grappling with what the restrictions could mean for their future. Her oldest daughter had talked about wearing the hijab one day, but now she’s weighing it against jobs that she may want to do.

“‘Either I give up on all these different positions that I can’t do or I don’t wear the hijab,’” she recalled her daughter telling her.

“And it’s just kind of up in the air,” said Waly. “I don’t have an answer for that.”

articles.title: Mexican leader rebukes US over DEA tip lines, claims ‘interference’
articles.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum rebuked U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials over its tip line, claiming it interfered with her country’s work. “The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum stated, according to the Associated Press. “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States…
articles.body:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum rebuked U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials over its tip line, claiming it interfered with her country’s work.

“The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum stated, according to the Associated Press . “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups.”

The Mexican president’s remarks came after she read parts of an Associated Press report , published on Tuesday, that alleged the DEA chose not to seize at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills while it tracked a drug trafficking ring for eight months. Amid the DEA’s inaction, the deadly drugs eventually flooded into the Southwest.

President Trump has attempted to pressure Sheinbaum to crack down on suspected cartel activity, while she accused him of undermining her leadership.

DEA Administrator Terry Cole also recently announced a tip line that encouraged people to report “members and associates of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs). Corrupt government officials providing material support to designated FTOs. Criminal networks and individuals laundering money to finance narcoterrorism.”

“Your information matters. Your identity and safety matter,” Cole wrote. “If you have information, connect with the DEA through the designated reporting channels.”

“Together, we can expose corruption, disrupt financial networks, dismantle narcoterrorist organizations, and protect our communities,” he concluded.

Sheinbaum asserted on Monday that U.S. officials were not allowed to operate on Mexican soil after it was discovered that the military flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to assist in capturing a top Sinaloa drug lord.

Authorities arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was on the FBI’s most wanted list . He was accused of manufacturing and distributing a large amount of methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin and marijuana, along with illegally possessing and using a firearm.

“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said, per the Associated Press .
